newsitem.title: USA: Freshmen battle as Republicans seek to hold House.
newsitem.headline: Freshmen battle as Republicans seek to hold House.

text.p: One week before Americans vote, Republicans are pulling out all the stops to try to retain the House of Representatives majority they won two years ago when 73 of their candidates swept into office for the first time.

Now some of those newcomers are fighting for their political lives, battered by their association with unpopular House Speaker Newt Gingrich and heavy campaign spending by the AFL-CIO labour organisation.

Of the 25 "most vulnerable" House members listed by the Capitol Hill newspaper Roll Call this week, 17 are Republican freshmen. "Politics Now," a joint effort of major news media, listed 25 freshmen races as too close to call.

With all polls showing Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole lagging far behind President Bill Clinton, Republicans this week opened a multi-million dollar advertising blitz to warn voters of the dire consequences of a Democratic election sweep of Congress and the presidency.

They predicted a resurgence of liberal policies unless congressional Republicans retained power to put a brake on a Clinton White House, echoing warnings that a Democratic majority in the House could propel a "radical roster" of Democrats into powerful committee chairmanships.

The current House party breakdown is 235-197, with one independent who usually votes with the Democrats, and two vacancies. Democrats need to pick up 19 seats to control the House. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47. All 435 House seats, and 34 Senate seats, are up for election.

Before 1994 Republicans last controlled both the House and Senate in the two-year Congress that ended in 1955. But the last election in which Republicans held on to a House majority in consecutive elections was in 1928.
Both sides were predicting gains in both the House and Senate, but independent analysts saw the House race as a tossup or favouring Republicans, with the Senate likely to remain in Republican hands.

The most dramatic Republican gain two years ago was in Washington state, where Republican freshmen grabbed six seats, including that of Democratic Speaker Tom Foley who was defeated by George Nethercutt.

Labour has been targeting some of these newcomers for special attention and this week Vice President Al Gore weighed in, appearing at a rally in Nethercutt's district to give a rousing speech for Democratic challenger Judy Olson.
Democrats hope to capture at least two and as many as four of the six seats. Nethercutt was not regarded as among the most vulnerable.
Also in the Pacific Northwest, Democrats were confident they would defeat Oregon freshman Jim Bunn and had an even chance of beating Idaho freshman Helen Chenoweth.

In Chicago, Republican Representative Michael Flanagan, who won the seat held by former House Ways and Means Chairman Dan Rostenkowski, later jailed for fraud, is trailing well behind his Democratic challenger Rod Blagojevich.

And in New York freshman Dan Frisa is lagging behind Carolyn McCarthy, a nurse turned gun control activist after her husband was killed and her son gravely injured during a massacre by a guman on a Long Island Rail Road commuter train in 1993.

Three of the House freshmen have already left the scene. Wes Cooley of Oregon and Enid Greene of Utah have quit, and a third, Sam Brownback, is in a close race for the presidential candidate Bob Dole's old Senate seat in Kansas.

The ad campaign launched by the National Republican Congressional Committee in about 50 key House districts asserts that a Democratic-run Congress in 1993 and 1994 pushed "the largest tax increase in history ... more wasteful Washington spending ... a government-run health care scheme."
Incumbent Republicans, including freshmen, are running in about half the 50 districts targeted by the Republican campaign, while the rest are open seats.
